newsitem.title: USA: Judge dismisses Silicon Graphics suit.
newsitem.headline: Judge dismisses Silicon Graphics suit.

text.p: A federal judge has dismissed a class-action lawsuit against Silicon Graphics Inc in a decision that could make it harder for investors to bring suits alleging stock market fraud, attorneys said on Friday.

The ruling, handed down last week by a U.S. District Court in San Francisco, has drawn the attention of securities lawyers and public companies because of the way it applies a new federal law aimed at blocking frivolous securities suits.
Attorney Bill Lerach, who represented investors in the Silicon Graphics lawsuit, said Friday that the ruling could be "devastating for investors."
"But it's not the end of the road," Lerach said, adding that he would appeal to the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals.
In a brief statement, Silicon Graphics said "We are gratified that the court's well-reasoned opinion appropriately ruled in our favor."
Attorney Bruce Vanyo, who represented Silicon Graphics in the case, said the ruling was a major victory "not only for Silicon Graphics but for Silicon Valley."
The lawsuit, filed in early 1996, alleged Mountain View, Calif.-based Silicon Graphics artificially inflated the price of its stock through false and misleading statements.

Last September, U.S. District Judge Fern Smith dismissed the lawsuit. Smith ruled that under the 1995 Private Securities Litigation Reform Act, shareholders who claimed that they lost money because of false and misleading information issued by a company must allege that there was "conscious behavior" by the company and must infer strongly that the company made "knowing" misrepresentations.

Those standards would be more difficult for shareholder plaintiffs to prove than claiming that misrepresentations were the result merely of "reckless behavior" by the companies, which had been sufficient grounds for plaintiffs to prevail.
Soon after the initial ruling, Lerach filed an amended class-action lawsuit against Silicon Graphics, providing the judge with more details about the alleged fraud.
The Securities and Exchange Commission in February filed a brief in support of the plaintiffs, urging the court to reconsider its position.
But in Smith's ruling, dated May 22, the judge once again dismissed the class-action lawsuit.
"After reviewing the arguments and the legal authorities, the court believes that its original interpretation was correct," Smith wrote in the ruling.
"The court finds that in order to state a private securities fraud claim, plaintiffs must create a strong inference of knowing or intentional misconduct," Smith wrote.

"Motive, opportunity, and non-deliberate recklessness may provide some evidence of intentional wrongdoing, but are not alone sufficient to support scienter (the mental state of intent) unless the totality of the evidence creates a strong inference of fraud," Smith said.
Lerach, with the law firm Milberg, Weiss, Bershad, Hynes & Lerach, said Smith's ruling would have serious ramifications for all stockholders if upheld on appeal.

"This opinion would make it virtually impossible for defrauded stockholders to go to federal court to recover damages and would all but completely insulate fraudsters in the securities markets from legal accountability," Lerach said.
Vanyo, of the law firm Wilson, Sonsini, Goodrich & Rosati, said the ruling should reduce the number of class-action lawsuits filed against public companies.
"Instead of filing lawsuits two days after a stock drops, they're going to have to go and investigate to find out if fraud took place," Vanyo said.
Lerach said if his appeal did not succeed in the appellate court, he would try to "take the case all the way to the Supreme Court of the United States."
